I can't speak for him or quote him exactly, but based on what he's said publicly in his books (*$100M Offers*, *$100M Leads*) and podcasts, his view would probably go something like this.

**He'd likely be skeptical of an MLM as a way to build wealth:**

- **You don't own anything.** He stresses building equity in an asset you control. In an MLM the company owns the product, the pricing, the brand and the compensation plan. They can change any of these, or shut down, and your "business" disappears.
- **The economics are bad for most people.** Independent analyses and many companies' own income disclosures show that most participants earn little or lose money once they count product purchases and expenses. Hormozi focuses on unit economics, so he'd ask what your real profit per hour is after costs. In most MLMs the honest answer is very low.
- **Recruiting replaces customers.** He says the business should be built on an offer so good people feel stupid saying no, sold to real buyers. When most of the money comes from recruiting other distributors, demand isn't real, and the market eventually runs out.
- **You can't make the offer better.** His whole framework is about increasing perceived value: the outcome, how likely it is, how fast it comes, and how much effort it takes. As a distributor you can't change the product, the price or the guarantee, so you're stuck selling a commodity, usually at a premium price.
- **It burns your relationships.** Selling mainly to friends and family uses up your "warm audience" quickly and can damage those relationships for good.

**He'd probably give some credit, though:**

- He's acknowledged that sales, outreach, handling rejection and personal development are valuable skills. Some people do learn to sell in an MLM, more than they would in a typical job.
- His likely framing: if you already learned those skills there, great. Now use them in something you own or in a job that pays you well to sell.

**What he'd likely recommend instead:**

1. **Get paid to learn sales.** For example, take a commission-based sales job, where you earn money and build skills without paying for inventory or starter kits.
2. **Pick a market with real pain and money to spend,** and build a service or offer you control.
3. **Start with simple outreach** (warm outreach, cold outreach, content) and keep reinvesting in skills and assets you own.
4. **Judge it as a business:** what it costs to get a customer, what a customer is worth over time, your margins, and whether it could keep running without you recruiting your way to income.

**In short,** he'd probably say an MLM can teach you to sell, but it's a poor vehicle for building wealth, because you're building someone else's asset under rules they can change at any time. If you want his actual words, search his YouTube channel or podcast for "MLM". He's discussed it directly in Q&As.

Almost certainly not, if you go by what he says publicly. I'm working from memory here and didn't look anything up.

**Why he'd skip it:**
- **He'd put the money back into the business.** His core advice is that early profit should go back into growth: better offers, lead generation and hiring. To him, $1M is an early milestone, not "made it" money.
- **He doesn't want luxuries to drain his capital.** He's said you should buy luxuries only when the returns on your money can pay for them, not the money itself. On that rule, $1M in profit is nowhere near Lambo territory.
- **He lives plainly.** He's known for wearing the same simple outfit every day, buying little, and saying that status purchases didn't make him happier.
- **He thinks long-term.** He has said he and his wife Leila deliberately lived below their means while building Gym Launch and Acquisition.com. Then they pushed toward much larger goals (Acquisition.com reports over $200M in yearly revenue across its companies) instead of cashing out early.

**The nuance:** He isn't against nice things. His view is roughly "buy the Lambo with the interest, not the principal." So he might buy one eventually, but only once his investments could cover it easily, not right after his first $1M.

If you want his exact words, his podcast (*The Game*) and his YouTube videos about spending and wealth cover this.

He'd probably be skeptical of a free-forever plan used as the main way to get users. He wouldn't reject free outright, though. His position is roughly: free is fine as a marketing tool, but it's a bad business model. This is my reading of his public work (*$100M Offers*, *$100M Leads*, *$100M Money Models*, and his podcast), not a quote.

## What he'd push back on

- **It brings in the wrong customers.** He often says that people who pay more complain less and get better results. Free plans tend to fill up with people who will never pay but still cost you support time and infrastructure.
- **It weakens his "value equation."** He says an offer's value depends on four things: how good the result is, how likely buyers think they are to get it, how long it takes and how much effort it needs. A $0 price undercuts the second one, because price signals quality and commitment. Customers who've paid tend to actually use what they bought.
- **It undercuts his rule of charging more.** His instinct is to raise prices and make the offer so good that people feel stupid saying no. "Free forever" teaches the market that your product is worth nothing.
- **It doesn't pay for acquisition.** In *Money Models* he argues that a new customer should pay back what it cost to get them, ideally within about 30 days. That's how you grow without running out of cash. A free-forever user brings in $0 by default, so you're paying to acquire them and hoping they upgrade someday.
- **There's no urgency.** If the free plan never ends, there's no reason to upgrade today, and he relies heavily on urgency and scarcity.

## Where he'd be fine with it

His lead-generation advice is to give away the secret and sell the implementation. A free tier can work as a **lead magnet** if it's built that way on purpose:

- It solves one narrow problem very well.
- Using it reveals the next problem, which only the paid plan solves.
- There's a planned path from free to paid: upsells, then cheaper fallback offers, then ongoing subscription offers.
- You count the cost of free users as marketing spend and track it against what each paying customer is worth over their lifetime.

## His likely advice to the founder

Something like: "Free isn't a business model, it's a marketing expense. If you want free, make it a lead magnet with a clear path to paying. Better still, try a paid trial, or a free trial that turns into paid, or a guarantee like 'you get results or your money back.' Then charge more than you think you should and back it with a guarantee that removes the risk of buying."

## Fair counterpoint

Some product-led SaaS companies have built big businesses on free tiers, including Slack, Dropbox, Notion and Figma. Free tends to work when sharing the product brings in new users, when serving one more user costs almost nothing, and when one free user can pull a paying team into the product. Hormozi's frameworks come mostly from high-touch, sales-led businesses like gyms, services and info products. So his critique hits hardest when your free users don't spread the product or lead to team-wide upgrades.

I can't point to a direct quote where Alex Hormozi answers this exact question, so this is my read of what he usually teaches, not his confirmed position.

**Probably not, unless the friend is actually the best person for the job.** These ideas from his content point that way:

- **Your first hire should buy back your time.** He says early hires should take over the low-value tasks that eat your time, or the ones you're bad at. The job comes first, then the person. Picking a friend first and fitting them into a role runs backwards.
- **You have to be able to fire them.** He stresses holding people to clear standards and acting quickly when someone isn't working out. If you're unwilling to fire your best friend, you've made a hire you can't manage. You also risk losing the friendship and the business together.
- **Character and fit matter more than familiarity.** He likes hiring people with a strong work ethic who can be trained. Being a friend doesn't prove either one.
- **Spell out the deal.** If you do hire someone close, he'd likely say to set expectations, metrics and consequences up front, and treat them exactly like any other employee.

**The other side:** Early on, trust and loyalty are worth a lot, and many founders do start with people they know. Hormozi himself runs Acquisition.com with his wife, Leila, so he isn't against mixing close relationships and business. He just expects them to be run with clear roles and accountability.

**In short:** He'd likely say hiring a friend is fine if they'd win the job on merit and you're both willing to treat it as a professional relationship, firing included. If you're hiring them because they're your friend, that's a red flag.

If you want his actual words, try searching his YouTube or podcast (*The Game*) for "hiring friends" or "first hire." He's covered first hires many times.

Here's what Alex Hormozi would probably say, based on *$100M Offers*, his Gym Launch years, and his content. These are his ideas in my words, not quotes.

**His likely verdict: "You're competing on price, which means you're losing."**

**1. Free brings in people who won't commit.**
People who pay, pay attention. A free month attracts tire-kickers who come twice and disappear. You also can't easily pitch them a full-price membership in week 4, because you've already taught them your service is worth $0.

**2. It's a discount, and he wants you to add value instead.**
His core rule is: don't lower the price, raise the value. Make the offer so good people would feel stupid saying no. Stack bonuses like a nutrition plan, an accountability coach, a progress check-in and a community group. Don't cut what you charge.

**3. You're paying to acquire clients when they could be paying you.**
Gym Launch was built on "client-financed acquisition." The first offer should bring in enough cash upfront to cover your ad spend and sales costs. A free month means you go into debt on every lead before you know whether they'll convert.

**4. What he'd suggest instead: a paid challenge with a strong guarantee.**
The classic Gym Launch move was a 6-week challenge:
- Paid upfront at a solid price.
- Includes a specific outcome, e.g. "lose X lbs in 6 weeks."
- Comes with a conditional guarantee: show up to every session, follow the plan, and if you don't hit the goal you get your money back, or it's credited toward a membership.
- Ends with an "ascension" pitch to continuing membership while results and motivation are at their peak.

That takes the risk off the customer without devaluing the product. It also screens for committed people, and the guarantee terms push them to actually show up, which is what produces results and retention.

**5. Your real problem probably isn't the price.**
He'd ask about your show-up rate, close rate and retention. A "free month" is often a patch over weak sales or onboarding. Fix the sales process and the first 30 days of the member experience before blaming price.

**In one line:** "Free is the most expensive price you can charge. Make it so good it's worth paying for, then take the risk away with a guarantee."

**One caveat he might add:** free or cheap front-end offers can work if you have a tight follow-up system that turns them into paying members. Most gym owners don't, so the promotion just burns money and coaching hours.

I can't quote him on this exact question, but he talks about money and skill-building a lot, so here's a fair summary of his likely take, based on views he's stated many times:

**1. "Your problem is income, not investing."**
He often says that if you have little money, investing returns don't matter much. 20% on $10k is $2k. Putting the same time into a skill that raises your income by $20k a year beats almost any trade. So he'd probably say to put the money and hours into earning more, not into trying to multiply savings you can't afford to lose.

**2. Ask how the teacher actually makes their money.**
He sells education himself, so he wouldn't knock courses in general. His test is whether the skill can earn you money in a market that pays reliably. If a "trader" makes their real money from course sales and not from trading, that tells you how well the strategy works.

**3. Day trading is a game you're unlikely to win.**
He favors "boring" wealth: build a business or a valuable skill, then park money in simple long-term investments. Day trading pits you against firms with better data, speed and capital. The research backs him up. A large study of Brazilian day traders (Chague et al., 2019) found that about 97% of those who kept at it for 300+ days lost money.

**4. Don't bet money you can't afford to lose.**
Your savings are your safety net and the runway that lets you take smart risks later, like starting something. Losing them puts you back at zero.

**What he'd likely tell you instead:** Keep your savings as savings. Spend a small amount, if anything, on learning a skill people pay for, like sales, marketing, a trade or a service. Use it to grow your income, and invest the extra boringly over the long term.

If you're still curious about crypto, a common middle ground is to use only money you'd be fine losing completely, and skip the course.

I don't know of any direct statement from Hormozi about a 4-day week for a 10-person agency, so this is an inference from his general views. **He most likely wouldn't recommend it as a default, but he wouldn't rule it out if the numbers held up.**

**Why he'd probably push back:**
- **Volume wins.** His "Rule of 100" and "more, better, new" framework say outworking competitors is the most reliable edge, especially early on. Cutting 20% of capacity cuts against that.
- **Agencies sell hours.** Delivery capacity sets revenue. If billable output drops, margins shrink, and margin is the number he cares about most.
- **Constraints first.** He'd ask what's actually holding the agency back: leads, sales, delivery or retention. Then he'd ask whether a 4-day week fixes that or is just a perk.
- **He prefers paying more.** He talks often about hiring "A-players", paying them well and giving them a path to grow. He'd likely prefer that over cutting hours.

**When he might accept it:**
- **Output per person holds.** He cares about outcomes, not hours at a desk. If you can show output, client results and margins stay the same, he'd treat it as a lever like any other.
- **You need it for hiring or retention.** If it helps you land and keep much better people than competitors can, it works as a hiring offer.
- **Your systems are mature.** It fits a stable, well-systematized agency better than one still finding its footing.

**How he'd probably say to test it:** Run it for a set period, such as one quarter. Track revenue per employee, delivery speed, client churn and profit margin. Keep it if the numbers hold and drop it if they don't, with no attachment to the idea either way.

If you want his actual words on the topic, search his YouTube channel or podcast (*The Game*) for "4 day work week". He's covered work ethic and team-building a lot, and he may have addressed it directly since my training data ends.

He'd almost certainly call it a mistake, unless the coach is already doing serious volume and the 12 products are deliberately built around one core offer.

**His main rule: one avatar, one offer, one channel.**
Hormozi says it a lot: until you're at roughly $1M+ a year, sell one product to one type of customer through one main acquisition channel. Twelve products at once breaks all three. He'd probably say something like *"You don't have 12 products, you have 12 half-built businesses."*

**What he'd say is going wrong:**
- **Split focus.** Every product needs its own marketing, sales script, delivery and improvements. A solo coach can't make 12 things great, so all 12 end up mediocre.
- **Confused buyers.** Too many choices slow people down or stop them buying. One clear offer that's obviously right for them converts better.
- **No reps.** You get good at selling and delivering by doing the same thing over and over. Twelve products spread those reps thin, so nothing improves quickly.
- **No proof.** With customers scattered across products, you don't build a stack of testimonials and case studies around one result.
- **Weak offers.** He'd likely bet that none of the 12 is a real "Grand Slam Offer" (from *$100M Offers*). Building more products is often a way to avoid fixing the one that should be working.

**The exception: a planned "money model."**
He isn't against having several products. In *$100M Money Models* he describes a structure built on purpose:
- **Attraction offer:** gets new customers in the door, often cheap or free.
- **Upsell / downsell:** something more (or less) offered at the moment of purchase.
- **Continuity:** a recurring subscription or membership.

The difference is that these all serve the **same customer**, run in a **set order**, and exist to raise customer value or lower acquisition cost. Twelve separate products launched side by side is the opposite of that.

**What he'd probably tell the coach to do:**
1. Find the one product with the best mix of demand, margin, results and ease of delivery.
2. Pause or cut the other 11, or fold the best parts into that one offer as bonuses.
3. Make that offer so good people "feel stupid saying no."
4. Push it through one channel until it's predictable.
5. Only then add an upsell or continuity offer for the same customers.

In short, he'd see 12 products as a focus problem disguised as a product strategy. This is my reading of the principles in his books and content, not a quote from him about this exact case.
